The old nation-states of Earth no longer exist. Instead, the United Nations has divided the planet into regional administrative zones, such as the West African Shared Interest Zone, the North American Shared Interest Zone, the Common European Interest Zone, the Maharshta-Karnataka-Goa Communal Interest Zone, the Persian Gulf Shared Interest Zone, the Balkan Shared Interest Zone, and the Pashwiri Autonomous Zone. These regional zones are determined by the “common interests” shared by the people living within them. Climate change has caused sea levels on Earth to rise, flooding many coastal cities and turning them whole or in part into crumbling, waterlogged ruins jutting from the sea. The asteroid impact in the Atlantic Ocean, and the ensuing tsunami, accelerated this inevitability. Most Atlantic coastal cities, even those with massive seawalls, were devastated and have either been abandoned or are still being rebuilt.

The Secretary-General

Leadership of Earth rests in the hands of the Secretary General of the United Nations, who has broad powers as chief execu tive and head of state. The secretary general serves as commander in chief of Earth’s military and commands the United Nations’ nuclear arsenal, though Earth’s nuclear capability was drastically reduced after it launched its entire complement of thousands of interplanetary nuclear missiles in an attempt to destroy Eros Station during its approach towards Earth. The United Nations Security Council, comprising the secretary general, the UN undersecretaries, and the admirals and generals commanding Earth’s military, holds executive authority over interplanetary matters involving other human polities in the system. Secretary General Chrisjen Avasarala assumed control of the government during the Free Navy Conflict, and her subse quent performance then ensured her reelection to the role of secretary-general after the Conflict ended. A shrewd and deter mined career politician, Avasarala worked the levers of power as Assistant Undersecretary of Executive Administration until her involvement in investigating the Ganymede Incident and the conspiracy in Earth’s government involving Protogen and protomolecule technology thrust her into the public eye. As Secretary-General, she now works tirelessly to help heal and

EARTH

Earth’s military, primarily the United Nations Navy and the United Nations Marine Corps, is still the most powerful combined military force in the system. Most of the UN Navy is spread throughout the solar system, overseeing and protecting Earth’s interests in the Belt and the Outers or keeping the peace as part of the Earth-Mars Coalition. While not as technologically advanced as the navy of the Martian Congressional Republic, the United Nations Navy is larger, consisting of capital ships such as dreadnoughts and battleships, as well as smaller vessels like cruisers, destroyers, frigates, corvettes, and more. Earth is still in the process of building new ships to replace those lost in recent military conflicts, but that has been a lower priority than the immediate needs of the planet’s inhabitants. The United Nations Marine Corps serves aboard UN Navy vessels and guards Earth outposts in the Belt and beyond. Marines wear vacuum-rated and radiation-shielded power armor, enabling them to engage in combat operations virtually anywhere in the system. The UNMC can place over 100 million troops on the battlefield, far outnumbering the ground forces of any other nation, including Mars, and the fact that UN marines are born, raised, live, and train in the one full gravity of Earth gives them a considerable advantage against opponents accustomed to the lower gravities of Mars or the Belt.

Earth remains, by far, the highest concentration of human population in the system. Although the Free Navy bombardment killed millions, and the infrastructure collapse that followed killed billions , Earth still has a population of some 29 billion to care for. Broadly, Earth’s citizens can be divided into two groups: those with jobs and those on Basic Assistance. The employed drive the economy, both with their purchasing power and their surplus production, which supports the rest of the planet’s population. Nevertheless, there are still sharp divisions even among the employed based on just how much money they have. The extremely wealthy live and shop in their own enclaves, with private security ensuring they never have to mingle with low- or middle-income earners, much less anyone on Basic. The employed have access to high-quality food and medical care, the ability to purchase land and property, and the right to have children, provided they can afford the license and taxes to do so. Instituted by the United Nations in an attempt to curb Earth’s overpopulation, the so-called “child tax” is prohibitively expensive, so it is not unheard of for groups of people to form civil unions or family co-ops where multiple parents share the tax burden (and even DNA) for one child. People on Basic tend to be uneducated and contribute little to Earth’s official economy, but they do engage in a vibrant barter economy among themselves, as well as having their own gray market industries and unlicensed services small enough to function without attracting much attention from the government. The only way off Basic is to get a job or an education. However, to apply to a university or other higher educational institution, a prospective student must have at least one year’s worth of work credits to demonstrate their commitment and work ethic, so educational resources and classroom space are not wasted on those who will not utilize them fully to contribute to society. There are uplift programs providing educational or job training opportunities for people on Basic who are self-taught or can meet strict entrance requirements, but they are highly competitive; waiting lists can be upwards of ten years long. As a result, these programs are only an option for a select few. For most people, life on Basic is the only one they will ever know, with the news, entertainment, and pornography feeds on their terminal screens and mood-altering drugs their only escape from their day-to-day existence. Unsurprisingly, many on Earth choose to seek a new life out among the stars beyond the Ring, volunteering for corpo-programs do not recruit many people on Basic Assistance, but the recruitment of Earth citizens with appropriate training or job experience opens up more opportunities for those on Basic to fill their spots, continuing the turnover. The same has been true of the loss of many people in urban areas along the Atlantic coasts, allowing Basic citizens from rural regions opportunities for training or work in reconstruction crews and the like.

The Unregistered

Regardless of class, both the employed and those on Basic are considered full citizens of the United Nations, their births and the details of their lives registered in countless government databases. Unofficially, however, there’s also a third class of people on Earth living at the margins of society, simply known as the ‘unregistered’. Whether the product of unlicensed birth or criminals who have erased all digital traces of their existence, the unregistered are united by the fact that there are no records of their lives. It’s therefore impossible to know exactly how many unregistered people live on Earth, eking out an existence in the cracks of society, but religious radicals and fringe groups are the source of most unregistered births, followed by the unlicensed children of the sex trade. Without even the rudimentary resources of those on Basic, the unregistered frequently live in the ruins of destroyed coastal cities and often turn to the black market and crime to support themselves. An unregistered can register themselves with the government at any time, though few choose to do so, instead preferring the freedom they enjoy that would be denied to them with a life on Basic—even if their unregistered existence is harder. Regional governments occasionally launch security sweeps of Basic housing and low-income or high-crime neighborhoods; any unregistered caught up in these sweeps are usually arrested and entered into the system. Those who refuse to provide their names for registration have new names assigned to them. Provided they’re not found guilty of some crime, they are registered on the Basic rolls and monitored by the government for the rest of their lives.

With such a high population, most of Earth’s citizens congregate in its teeming cities that sprawl across the planet’s surface. At one time, the Urban Arcology movement attempted to address Earth’s overpopulation problem by building vast structures to house dense concentrations of people with minimal impact on their surrounding environment. Powered by their own self-contained fusion reactors, these arcologies were designed to exist as self-sustaining ecosystems, but the technology did not yet exist to fully exploit the concept. Nevertheless, failed arcologies litter many cities on Earth, towering into the sky or stretching for miles through the urban landscape. Some people still inhabit the crumbling monoliths from a more optimistic time, but the Urban Arcology movement never lived up to its promise. Today, most cities have a central commercial district, filled with skyscrapers housing corporate offices and luxury resi - dential apartments for the wealthy. Basic and minimal-income housing neighborhoods ring the commercial districts and stretch for kilometers, making up the largest proportion of real estate in most cities. Even with this much area, space is at a premium. Basic housing is crowded, and government apartment blocks are often old, underfunded, and derelict. Shared accommodations are usually mandated, and extended families inhabit living spaces designed for half as many people. Low-income homes are an improvement over Basic housing, consisting of either simple apartments or small, mass-produced, single-story houses on tiny plots of land. They are only distinct, however, in that their residents pay rent or mortgages and thus get some say over their condition and location. Finally, on the outskirts of the cities sit the orderly grids of middle-income suburbs and strip malls. Streets are invariably crowded with automated traffic and the packed throngs of people, either those with jobs traveling to and from work at shift change or the aimless masses on Basic, wandering the streets and searching for some meaning in their lives. The open land outside of Earth’s sprawling urban centers is dedicated to mostly automated industrial farming, where machines labor to produce the food and other organics to sustain not only Earth’s population, but much of the solar system as well. Private land ownership is rare outside the ranks of the ultra-wealthy, though small family farms do persist in some areas, contributing their own tiny share to the planet’s total food production. The vast frontier opened by the Ring network —Nemesis Games has strengthened this urge to leave the nest and explore, especially given the opportunity to travel to other planets that offer the Earth-like comfort of a breathable atmosphere and something close to Earth-normal gravity. The same dreams and ambitions carried the ancestors of the Martians and the Belters on their initial voyages, although Earth’s relationship with her colonial children has not always been easy, nor even cordial. For a long time, Earth treated its colony on Mars as an afterthought, then felt betrayed when Martians bartered for their independence. Earthers often see Martians as arrogant and narrow-minded, obsessed with their grand endeavor, and willing to give up their freedoms and suborn themselves to the cause.

To a citizen of Mars, where unem- Threat: Moderate ployment is almost nonexistent, the idea that someone can sit around doing nothing day after day but watching entertainment feeds while waiting for their government handout is almost unbelievable. Of course, life on Mars is difficult and the planet is inhospitable to human life, whereas Earth has air, water, resources, and the capacity to allow half of its citizens to live off the excess, a luxury Mars may never know. Although Earthers and Martians haven’t necessarily settled their differences, the changes in the system have softened them somewhat. A battered and damaged Earth is no longer quite the luxury it once was, and a diminished and depopulated Mars no longer focuses quite so clearly on its great endeavor. Both Inner Planets have become more interdependent, on each other and on the Transport Union and the flow of resources from the Belt, the outer planets, and the extrasolar colonies.

Luna is Earth’s only natural satellite. It is only a quarter of Earth’s diameter, with a gravity of 0.16 g, lighter than many spin stations in the Belt. At only 384,402 kilometers away from Earth, Luna was the site of humanity’s first landing on another planet, as well as the location of Earth’s first interplanetary colony, established in the early 21st century. This first permanent lunar base was a shared military and scientific endeavor, and while elements of both remain, Luna is now much more of a civilian station. Like Earth, Luna is governed by the United Nations, and its approximately one billion inhabitants are UN citizens. Basic Assistance does not extend to Luna, however, so its citizens are generally wealthier than their counterparts on Earth. Lunar natives tend to have thinner frames—a result of life in low gravity—but are not as tall and thin as their Belter cousins. Luna functions as a waystation between Earth and the rest of the solar system, more so now than ever, and serves as a natural meeting place between residents of the Inner Planets and inhabitants of the Belt and Outers. Due to its low gravity, Luna is the only planet in the Inner System that Belters can easily visit and where they can comfortably remain for any substantial length of time. Just as on Earth, Luna hosts numerous corporate headquarters as well as respected universities and scientific institutes. It is a hub for commerce and travel with frequent shuttle flights to and from Earth as well as regular long-hau l transport and passenger service to the Outers. With no atmosphere, Luna is subject to intense solar radiation and a constant rain of micro-meteors, so surface domes like those on Mars would be a significant risk. As a result, virtually all of Luna’s habitats and infrastructure are underground, although high resolution screens serve as “windows” offering views of the lunar surface. Only Luna’s spaceport and access ports to the subterranean tunnels are above ground. As Earth’s oldest non-terrestrial settlement, much of Luna Station is old and worn, though of course newer construction has been added in the intervening centuries. A unique feature of Luna is a smell like gunpowder in the air, the result of lunar dust that manages to pass through even the finest air filters over time.

Lovell City

Luna’s largest settlement and de facto capital, Lovell City, spreads out around the primary spaceport, though little of the city is visible from the surface. Just like its sister cities on Earth, Lovell City contains warehouses, commercial centers, office complexes, shipyards, convention centers, hotels, prisons, residential areas, and schools. Pedicabs and electric carts carry passengers on short trips through the city’s tunnels, but mass transit tube stations stretch throughout Lovell City, connecting its farther-flung districts. Lovell City’s spaceport is unique in the system, its ancient docks dug out of the lunar surface. Tugs guide vessels in and out of the docks, which are large enough to house entire ships within them. Unlike in the spin stations of the Belt, where vessels sit in vacuum while docked, Luna’s docks have retractable seals, allowing them to be filled with air so maintenance and repair crews can work on the parked ships without full vac suits, although their helmets are always close at-hand in case of a breach.

New Hague

New Hague is a district in Lovell City containing Luna’s United Nations complex, including administrative offices and courts, that has become the prime administrative facility for the UN since the Free Navy Conflict. The General Assembly still meets in Geneva, but most UN business gets done from a place overlooking Earth. The United Nations Science Service is based in New Hague as well, which has had a presence on Luna since the original moon base; they constructed the first broad-array telescope on the moon, free from the distorting effects of Earth’s atmo - sphere. Over the centuries, however, the frontiers of science moved to the Outers, leaving the UN Science Service a shadow of its former self, but exploration through the Ring gate has revitalized the UN station, which now serves as a hub for gathering, cataloging, and analyzing data from the exploration of hundreds of new star systems and planets. The UN Navy maintains a local military presence at Luna Base, where UN Marines train in the low lunar gravity to accustom themselves to operations in vacuum and low-gravity worlds. Earth’s primary shipbuilding facilities, the Bush Orbital Shipyards, are in orbit around Luna. The shipyards build most of the UN Navy’s warships as well as a large number of civilian ships. Only the Transport Union facilities in the Belt and Outer Planets currently have the capacity to construct larger vessels.

The solar system’s second planet, Venus is similar in size and mass to Earth, but strikingly different in almost every other way. Venus has a retrograde rotation, opposite the counter-clockwise rotations of most of the solar system’s other planets, and its rotational period of 243 days is the slowest of all the planets. This means that Venus’s day is longer than its year of 224.7 days. Although Venus’s gravity is only slightly less than that of Earth’s, the planet’s dense carbon dioxide atmosphere results in a crushing 92 atmospheres of pressure on its surface. It also creates a powerful greenhouse effect, leading to surface temperatures of 735 K, making Venus the hottest planet in the solar system—hotter even than the surface of Mercury. Although it was the first planet to be visited and landed on by unmanned spacecraft from Earth, Venus has never been colonized—by humans, at least. No cities were ever built in the skies above Venus, no colonists arrived, —Caliban’s Warand the whole endeavor is now viewed as an epic failure in interplanetary colonization. The attention of the entire solar system turned to Venus, however, when Eros Station crashed into the planet’s surface. Having traveled into the inner solar system from the Belt at almost impossible speeds, Eros halted in orbit above Venus, then split apart into hundreds of identical pieces that spread across the planet, depositing the extraterrestrial protomolecule on the surface. There the protomolecule “cooked” and underwent a bizarre transformation, building two-kilometer tall crystalline towers, as well as a network of interconnected filament hexagons each fifty kilometers across that carry electrical currents and superheated water. The UN dispatched the science ship Arboghast to investigate the protomolecule’s crash-site on Venus, wherein they discovered that Mars had also sent a ship to gather information. Both ships were lost almost immediately. The final transmissions from the Arboghast indicated the protomolecule somehow disassembled the entire ship—and its crew—piece by piece, possibly absorbing them into its mass. No further ships were sent. A little over a year later, the protomolecule construction on Venus reached a critical mass—and left. It launched itself back into space in the form of a “squid”-like vessel that traveled to the outer reaches of the solar system to form the Ring. It is widely believed that every trace of the protomolecule on Venus left with it, along with a substantial portion of the planet’s metals and other natural resources. Still, the system warily watches the clouds of the second planet in case there’s something hidden just beneath the surface, another unseen alien terror biding its time.

9: Mars ettled in the 21st century after a number of lengthy exploratory missions, Mars was a world of dreamers devoted to a single vision: the greening of the red planet. It is a world of survivors, eking out every last erg of efficiency in a centuries-long battle against an environment never meant for human life. Mars may be a stillborn world, a dream that is dying, unlikely to survive unless something changes, but it is a world of warriors, believing themselves stronger, smarter, and more determined than everything else under the sun. For generations, Martians focused solely on their Great Endeavor: terraforming the planet into an environment able to sustain life. Those generations all knew they would never see the fruits of their labor, but they believed in the work and in the wisdom of planting seeds for the future—at least, until recently. The opening of the Ring gates and the discovery of more than a thousand life-bearing worlds made the dream of a living Mars seem quaint and naive by comparison. Why work your whole life to raise life from a dead, red desert when you could take that same bold, colonizing spirit to a new, already Earth-like world? That’s certainly the conclusion Admiral Duarte and his followers came to when they decided in secret to desert the Martian Navy along with a third of its personnel, ships, and equipment, going through the Ring and claiming the Laconia system as their own. The exodus of the so-called “First Fleet” was a blow to Martian morale the proud red planet has yet to recover from—and may never do. From its peak of some four billion, Mars’s population has declined for the first time in its history, and continues to do so as Martians seek their fortunes elsewhere beyond the Ring, their skills in building frontier colonies in high-demand. Those left behind are either fiercely dedicated to a dream that’s increasingly unrealistic, unable to leave even if they want to, or find there are different opportunities on a planet that’s increasingly hopeless, lawless, and empty.

“Earth. Mars. They’re not that different,” Miller said. “Try telling that to a Martian,” Havelock said with a bitter laugh.

The first Martians were colonists from Earth, scientists, explorers, and engineers.
